strengths: The paper proposes an intuitive and technically interesting formulation: representing instances as colors and training with permutation-invariant intra-instance consistency and inter-instance separation losses. This provides a simple way to adapt image-generative architectures without a conventional mask decoder.

The reported cross-domain generalization is compelling. Stable Diffusion variants obtain strong single-point mIoU across COCOexc, art, egocentric, fine-structure, and X-ray datasets, including a substantial advantage over SAM on iShape.

Evaluating both Stable Diffusion and MAE encoder-decoder models is useful evidence that the phenomenon is not solely attributable to internet-scale text-image training. The SD-Limited experiment also partially addresses leakage through unknown-category annotations.

The paper includes several informative comparisons, a component ablation, an edge-detection experiment, and extensive qualitative results. The qualitative examples support the claim that the representations preserve boundaries and compositional structure.
The method and training setup are explained clearly, with useful implementation details, computational costs, category counts, and stated plans to release code and checkpoints.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that generative pretraining uniquely produces transferable instance grouping—is not adequately isolated. DINO-B is coupled to a custom, minimally described up-convolution/VAE decoder, while SimpleClick introduces substantial architectural and optimization differences. Stronger controls such as DINOv2, iBOT, other masked-image models, discriminative backbones with matched decoders, and pretrained-versus-random or encoder-only-versus-decoder ablations are missing.

Despite the broad instance-segmentation framing, the main evaluation is interactive segmentation with a ground-truth-derived center prompt. The paper does not evaluate automatic instance discovery, proposal recall, AP, or the conversion of the full color image into a set of instances. Thus, the evidence supports transferable promptable features more directly than general-purpose instance segmentation.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. SAM is the only broadly pretrained promptable reference; newer or alternative foundation segmentation models are absent. Figure 5 excludes COCO medium and small objects—precisely the principal failure regime—and reports averaged relative recovery rather than complete per-dataset results or standard interactive-segmentation measures.

The definition of 'unseen' is not consistently rigorous. Standard SD training includes roughly 30% unknown-category masks, COCOexc exclusions rely partly on manual verification, and claims that some domains or objects were absent from pretraining are speculative. SD-Limited helps but does not fully establish absence of relevant visual concepts from pretraining.

There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated-run results, statistical tests, or clear evaluation sample counts. It is also unclear whether thresholds and other post-processing choices were selected on held-out validation data; the fixed threshold and bilateral filtering may materially affect comparisons.

The paper overinterprets several observations. Poor performance of the selected discriminative baselines does not establish that the effect is exclusive to generative models, and edge precision at only the low-recall portion of a curve does not substantiate general superiority in boundary localization. Standard BSDS ODS/OIS/AP reporting and better-controlled edge baselines would strengthen this claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite substantial implementation detail: the efficient computation of losses over as many as 1,250 instances, exact preprocessing and sampling rules, prompt/post-processing implementation, and model-selection protocol are not specified sufficiently to independently reproduce all results.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting direction: repurposing pretrained generative models for category-agnostic instance segmentation using limited synthetic supervision.
The instance-coloring objective is intuitive and avoids assigning arbitrary fixed colors to instances; the component ablation indicates that its variance and separation terms are useful.

Evaluation spans several substantially different domains, including natural images, artwork, egocentric scenes, intricate structures, and X-rays. The appendix also provides extensive qualitative results.

The reported performance on large objects and iShape is promising, and the comparison between MAE-B and the similarly pretrained SimpleClick backbone suggests that retaining and adapting generative decoding features may be valuable.
The training setup, principal hyperparameters, data composition, and object-category lists are documented reasonably well.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that generative pretraining inherently produces the observed grouping ability—is not adequately isolated. SimpleClick changes the decoder, objective, and inference procedure, while DINO-B uses an ad hoc DINO-to-VAE architecture. Missing controls include training from scratch, an encoder-only MAE with a matched decoder, frozen versus finetuned generative features, and discriminative and generative models with genuinely matched architectures and capacity.

The paper overstates zero-shot generalization. All models receive 3.7 million instance masks during finetuning, including roughly 1.38 million masks assigned an unknown class. SD-Limited ignores regions inside unknown-mask bounding boxes, but this does not establish absence of relevant visual supervision or pretraining exposure. Assertions that some domains are absent from ImageNet are based on speculation rather than an auditable overlap analysis.

The headline comparison with SAM is selective. SD only matches SAM on COCO large objects, while trailing severely on medium and small objects; it also remains substantially behind SAM on most other datasets. The multi-prompt summary excludes precisely the COCO medium and small regimes where the method performs worst, weakening the broad claim of approaching SAM.

The baseline suite is too narrow for the paper's general-purpose segmentation claims. It omits SAM2 and other strong promptable or category-agnostic segmentation systems, as well as more relevant diffusion-feature and unsupervised grouping approaches. SAM inference settings are also insufficiently specified to ensure a controlled comparison.

Evaluation relies heavily on ground-truth-derived prompts: the first point is the ground-truth object center, and subsequent points are selected through oracle access to the largest remaining ground-truth error region. This measures response under an idealized interaction policy rather than autonomous instance segmentation, despite broader language throughout the paper.

The quantitative evidence is incomplete. Dataset sample counts and uncertainty are not reported; there are no multiple runs or confidence intervals; edge detection is presented mainly as a curve without standard ODS, OIS, or AP values; and robustness to the global similarity threshold, bilateral filtering, prompt placement, and output normalization is not studied.

The prompting rule is under-specified and potentially fragile: inverse squared distance is singular when a feature equals the query, min-max normalization can be dominated by outliers, and the very small fixed threshold is not justified across models and datasets.

The paper makes further unsupported interpretive claims, including that the outputs reveal hierarchical scene representations and that discriminative pretraining generally fails because it emphasizes invariance. The presented colors and two mismatched baselines do not establish these conclusions.

Although the qualitative outputs are often compelling, they also reveal substantial under-segmentation, merging, coarse boundaries, and missed small objects. The discussion tends to interpret these failures as emergent perceptual preferences rather than testing alternative explanations such as resolution, loss bias, or thresholding.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the causal thesis and broad generalization claims are stronger than the controlled evidence. The missing matched baselines and selectively summarized evaluation are substantial enough to place the paper below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and interesting central finding: generatively pretrained Stable Diffusion and MAE encoder-decoder models can be fine-tuned on a narrow synthetic distribution yet transfer to previously unsupervised object categories and substantially different visual domains.

The instance-coloring formulation is simple, intuitive, and well motivated. Its permutation-invariant combination of intra-instance consistency and inter-instance separation provides a practical way to adapt RGB-generating architectures to instance grouping.

The evaluation covers five meaningfully different datasets—including art, egocentric imagery, intricate shapes, and X-rays—plus BSDS500 edge detection. The results consistently favor the proposed generative models over the included limited-supervision baselines.

Several results are genuinely compelling: Stable Diffusion nearly matches SAM on large unseen COCO objects and DRAM, exceeds it on iShape, and MAE transfers surprisingly well despite ImageNet-1K-only pretraining and 224×224 fine-tuning.

The paper includes useful controls and analysis: a category-limited Stable Diffusion variant, same-backbone comparison between MAE-B and SimpleClick, a discriminatively pretrained DINO-B baseline, loss-component ablations, randomly selected qualitative pages, and transparent discussion of small-object failures.

The manuscript is clearly written, visually persuasive, and reasonably reproducible, with training hyperparameters, data composition, category lists, resource requirements, and claimed code/model availability documented.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate generative pretraining as the cause of generalization. DINO-B uses a custom DINO-to-VAE architecture with a single up-convolution, while SimpleClick has a different decoder and training objective. A controlled comparison using identical architectures and capacity with generative versus discriminative pretraining is needed to support the paper's strongest causal claim.

The quantitative task is oracle-prompted mask extraction using ground-truth object centers, rather than automatic category-agnostic instance segmentation. There are no standard AP, AR, or proposal-recall results, so the broad title and some claims about general-purpose instance segmentation exceed what is directly demonstrated.

SAM is the only strong general-purpose comparator. Given that SAM2 is discussed and other promptable or open-world segmentation systems exist, broader comparisons would make the competitiveness claim more convincing.

The reported tables provide point estimates without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical testing. This matters for close comparisons such as SD versus SAM and for establishing the stability of fine-tuning.

Claims of transfer to styles or pixels never encountered during pretraining are not verifiable from ImageNet-1K and web-scale data provenance. The defensible claim is absence of segmentation supervision for those domains, not necessarily absence of similar images during pretraining.

The prompt decoding procedure contains underspecified numerical and evaluation details, including stabilization of the inverse-distance similarity, normalization, threshold selection, sensitivity to its hyperparameters, and precise handling of multiple prompts. Reproducibility would benefit from an ablation of this post-processing.

Performance remains very weak for medium and especially small COCO objects, and the nine-prompt average explicitly excludes these cases. This narrows the practical generality of the method and should be reflected more prominently in the conclusions.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting and potentially important empirical finding: generatively pretrained MAE and Stable Diffusion models can be adapted using masks from narrow synthetic domains and still transfer to unseen object categories and substantially different visual domains.

The instance-coloring formulation is simple, architecture-agnostic, and reasonably motivated. The component ablation demonstrates that the intra-instance, pixel-separation, and mean-separation terms each contribute.

Evaluation spans several meaningfully different domains, including artwork, egocentric imagery, irregular structures, and X-rays. Results on iShape are particularly compelling, with Stable Diffusion substantially outperforming SAM for fine structures.

The study includes useful analyses of training-category diversity, alternative fine-tuning datasets, image perturbations, diffusion timesteps, prompt count, and the number of fine-tuned layers. The decoder-only result provides suggestive evidence that useful grouping information resides in generatively pretrained decoder features.

The paper is generally clear, visually compelling, and comparatively transparent about limitations such as poor small-object performance and incomplete edge recall. Implementation details and compute requirements are provided.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that the observed transfer is specifically due to generative pretraining—is not established convincingly. DINO+VAE is an architecturally mismatched control with a newly learned connector, while SimpleClick has a randomly initialized task decoder. Missing controls include randomly initialized versions of the same architectures, discriminatively pretrained models with comparably pretrained high-resolution decoders, frozen-feature evaluations, and stronger modern self-supervised or generative-feature baselines.

The main comparison is almost exclusively against SAM v1. The paper cites SAM2 but does not evaluate it, and omits other recent promptable, category-agnostic, open-world, or diffusion-based segmentation methods. Thus, the evidence is insufficient to establish competitiveness with the current state of the art.

The edge-detection claim relies on AP restricted to recall below 20%, an unusual metric selected because the proposed models perform poorly at higher recall. High precision on a small subset of easy boundaries does not substantiate the broader claims that the models consistently produce better or crisper boundaries than SAM. Standard full-range edge metrics should also be reported.

Prompt extraction introduces consequential hand-designed post-processing—Gaussian query averaging, per-image normalization, bilateral filtering, and a fixed threshold—but sensitivity to these choices is not evaluated. It is also unclear how the threshold and other evaluation hyperparameters were selected without tuning on the test domains.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical tests. Sample counts and aggregation details are not clearly reported for most evaluation datasets, making it difficult to assess the robustness of sometimes modest differences.

The category-diversity experiments contain confounds: the 5- and 10-class Stable Diffusion variants receive half as many training iterations, ignored objects are removed using bounding boxes, and the alternative training datasets differ simultaneously in image domain, annotation quality, complexity, and category coverage. Consequently, these experiments do not cleanly isolate supervision diversity.

Performance remains very weak on medium and especially small COCO objects, where Stable Diffusion obtains 38.8 and 8.5 mIoU versus SAM's 59.5 and 56.9. The abstract and conclusion overstate overall competitiveness with SAM without sufficiently qualifying this major limitation.

Although the empirical phenomenon is promising, the loss closely follows prior discriminative embedding objectives and the paper explicitly disclaims methodological novelty. Given the incomplete controls and limited baseline coverage, the current evidence falls slightly short of supporting the broad scientific conclusion that generative models inherently learn a uniquely general grouping mechanism.

strengths: The paper asks an interesting and relevant question: whether generative pretraining supplies transferable object-grouping priors when mask supervision covers only a restricted set of categories.

The empirical scope is broader than a single benchmark: MAE and Stable Diffusion variants are evaluated across natural images, artwork, egocentric scenes, irregular structures, X-rays, and boundary detection.

Several ablations are useful, including loss-component removal, training-category diversity, alternative fine-tuning datasets, color perturbations, diffusion timestep, and the number of fine-tuned layers.

The Stable Diffusion model obtains notable results on large COCO objects and especially iShape, while the decoder-only MAE result provides suggestive evidence that pretrained generative representations contain useful grouping information.

The instance-coloring formulation is simple, architecture-agnostic, and produces visually compelling dense groupings. The manuscript is generally readable and includes extensive qualitative results. weaknesses: The central causal conclusion—that generalization is inherent or unique to generative pretraining—is not established. The paper compares against only one discriminative representation setup, DINO-B plus a newly attached VAE pathway, and one interactive architecture, SimpleClick. These differ in architecture, capacity, decoder initialization, resolution, and optimization from the strongest models. Controlled comparisons using identical architectures and decoders with generative versus discriminative pretraining, random initialization, encoder-only MAE features, and stronger modern discriminative/self-supervised representations are needed.

The SAM comparison is repeatedly presented more favorably than the complete results support. Stable Diffusion only slightly exceeds SAM for large COCO objects and substantially exceeds it on iShape, but is markedly worse on medium and small COCO objects, EgoHOS, and PIDRay. For example, small-object mIoU is 8.5 versus 56.9. Consequently, claims of broadly approaching heavily supervised SAM require substantial qualification.

The edge-detection headline relies on a nonstandard truncated metric—AP only below 20% recall. The appendix explicitly shows that performance deteriorates at higher recall because the method fails to represent many annotated regions. Reporting the favorable initial portion as evidence that the method outperforms SAM does not establish superior overall boundary detection; standard full-range ODS/OIS/AP and boundary-localization metrics are necessary.

The baseline set is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Relevant category-agnostic, unsupervised/pseudo-label, diffusion-feature, and newer promptable segmentation methods are discussed but not evaluated. SimpleClick's extremely low scores also warrant diagnostic validation, since a near-total baseline failure is carrying considerable argumentative weight.

The claimed supervision regime is semantically narrow but not small: it contains 86,000 images and roughly 3.7 million instance masks, including about 1.38 million instances assigned to an 'unknown' class. This weakens the limited-experience narrative and makes the precise absence of target-like shapes difficult to audit. Moreover, target categories can occur in ImageNet or internet-scale generative pretraining, so the result is zero-shot with respect to mask labels, not visual exposure.

The experiments lack uncertainty estimates, repeat runs, or significance analysis. Several conclusions are based on small differences, while some variants were trained for only half as many iterations, creating an avoidable comparison confound.

Important evaluation and reproduction details are incomplete or insufficiently validated, including dataset-level sample counts, treatment of center prompts that fall outside irregular masks, complete preprocessing/inference specifications, threshold-selection methodology, optimizer details, and sensitivity to the hand-designed prompting and post-processing pipeline.

Claims about hierarchical part-whole representations are based primarily on subjective color similarities in selected examples and receive no quantitative evaluation. Similarly, explanations involving equivariance, text-conditioning bias, and generative models 'defaulting' to clean edges are hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

Overall, the work contains a promising empirical observation, but the inadequate controls, weak baseline coverage, selective edge metric, and overstatement of causal conclusions prevent it from being competitive at a top-tier venue in its current form.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and compelling finding: generatively pretrained models can be adapted using masks from a narrow set of categories and still produce useful instance groupings for substantially different object types and visual domains.

The instance-coloring formulation is simple, architecture-agnostic, and well motivated. Although related embedding losses are not claimed as novel, applying this formulation to preserve and expose generative representations is an effective design choice.

The evaluation covers five meaningfully different domains, including artwork, egocentric imagery, fine structures, and X-rays. Stable Diffusion approaches SAM on several single-click evaluations and substantially exceeds it on iShape, despite using far less mask supervision.

The MAE results are especially informative because they demonstrate transfer without internet-scale text-image pretraining. Comparisons against DINO-B and SimpleClick provide evidence that the result is not explained solely by the synthetic fine-tuning data or the MAE encoder initialization.

The paper includes useful ablations over loss components, training categories, training datasets, diffusion timesteps, image perturbations, and fine-tuning depth. The decoder-only result strengthens the hypothesis that grouping information is already present in generatively pretrained representations.

The paper is clearly written, visually convincing, candid about poor small-object performance, and provides substantial qualitative evidence alongside quantitative results. Implementation and training details are reasonably extensive.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that generalization is specifically due to generative pretraining—is not fully isolated. The DINO+VAE baseline is a particular hybrid with a newly learned connector and is not a comprehensive test against modern discriminative or self-supervised dense representations. Comparisons to additional strong backbones and feature-grouping methods would make this conclusion more convincing.

The term “zero-shot” requires careful qualification: the evaluated categories are unseen in mask fine-tuning, but they are likely abundant in Stable Diffusion pretraining and often present in ImageNet pretraining. The experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer of segmentation supervision, not necessarily visual recognition of previously unseen categories.

The headline comparison to SAM is incomplete. The proposed model remains far behind SAM on medium and small COCO objects, and the multi-click evaluation recovers only about 82% of SAM after nine clicks. Consequently, claims of broadly comparable segmentation performance should be restricted mainly to large objects and selected out-of-domain settings.

The edge experiment emphasizes AP only below 20% recall, an unusual truncated metric that favors the proposed models. The full curves show that their coverage deteriorates markedly at higher recall because many regions are never segmented. Standard full-range boundary metrics should be reported prominently, with truncated AP treated as supplementary analysis.

The prompt evaluation uses ground-truth object-center clicks and a custom fixed-threshold extraction procedure. More standard interactive-segmentation protocols, threshold sensitivity, per-dataset sample counts, and statistical variation across training runs are missing.

The baseline set omits several relevant alternatives, such as more recent promptable segmenters, unsupervised instance-segmentation/grouping systems, and stronger contemporary generative backbones. There is also no matched control that varies generative versus discriminative pretraining while holding architecture, decoder, resolution, and parameter count as constant as possible.

Some qualitative and conceptual claims—particularly emergent part-whole compositionality and “inherent” grouping—are supported mainly by selected visual examples rather than a quantitative evaluation. These are intriguing observations but currently stronger as hypotheses than established conclusions.

Reproducibility is promising because code and checkpoints are stated to be available, but the manuscript does not report uncertainty, inference cost, evaluation-set cardinalities, or how the global prompting threshold was selected. No major ethical concern is apparent, although downstream safety-critical applications mentioned in the paper would require substantially stronger validation.
